title: Philosophies of Mathematics — Platonism · Formalism · Nominalism · Structuralism (One‑Pager + Bios)
content_html:
Philosophies of Mathematics

Platonism · Formalism · Nominalism · Structuralism

Platonism

Mathematical entities (numbers, sets, shapes) exist independently of minds; truths are timeless.

Ontology: Abstract objects in a non-spatiotemporal realm.
Epistemology: Access via rational insight; raises Benacerraf’s causal-access problem.
View of proof: Reveals eternal truths; proofs discover, not invent.
Strengths: Explains universality & stability; fits Wigner’s “effectiveness”.
Critiques: How do we know abstract things? Ontological extravagance.

Example lens: π existed before humans; prime numbers “out there.”

Plato (c. 428–348 BCE) - Classical Greek philosopher who posited a realm of perfect, eternal Forms (Ideas). In dialogues like Republic and Phaedo, the Form of mathematical objects grounds their necessity and universality. This metaphysical backdrop inspires modern mathematical Platonism.

Formalism

Mathematics is symbolic manipulation under axioms; meaning is secondary to consistency.

Ontology: No commitment to abstract objects; just strings and derivations.
Epistemology: Knowledge = derivability in formal systems.
View of proof: Proofs are rule-governed transformations.
Strengths: Precision; clear standards; avoids mysterious realms.
Critiques: Gödel shows limits of completeness/consistency; where does meaning come from?

Example lens: ZFC set theory, Peano arithmetic as rigorously defined systems.

David Hilbert (1862–1943) - German mathematician who championed the axiomatization of mathematics and the program to prove consistency and completeness of formal systems. His work on foundations and the 1900 list of problems shaped 20th‑century formal approaches, even as Gödel later revealed inherent limits.

Nominalism

No abstract mathematical objects; mathematics is a human-made language for organizing experience.

Ontology: Only concrete particulars; “numbers” are names/conveniences.
Epistemology: Learn math like language; tied to practice and culture.
View of proof: Socially sanctioned derivations within a practice.
Strengths: Metaphysically modest; aligns with cognitive and cultural accounts.
Critiques: Struggles with physics’ precision; why cross-cultural convergence?

Example lens: “2” is a useful label; sets are fictions aiding science.

Hartry Field (b. 1946) - American philosopher who advanced a nominalist program in Science Without Numbers (1980), arguing that scientific theories can be reformulated without quantifying over abstract mathematical entities, thereby deflating ontological commitment.

Structuralism

What’s real are structures/relations; objects are positions in structures.

Ontology: Commitment to structural patterns (e.g., group, field, category), not individual abstract “things.”
Epistemology: Know structures via invariants, mappings, and equivalences.
View of proof: Exhibits structural relationships (isomorphism, functoriality).
Strengths: Matches modern math (category theory); dovetails with scientific structural realism.
Critiques: What are structures “made of”? Risk of collapsing into Platonism or deflationary views.

Example lens: Natural numbers as positions in the ω-sequence; groups defined up to isomorphism.

Stewart Shapiro (b. 1951) - American philosopher whose Philosophy of Mathematics: Structure and Ontology (1997) articulates ante rem structuralism: structures exist independently of systems instantiating them; mathematical objects are positions in those structures.

James Ladyman (b. 1968) & Don Ross (b. 1960) - Philosophers co‑authoring Everything Must Go (2007), advocating naturalized metaphysics and structural realism in science: prioritize relational and model-based structure over entity‑based metaphysics; influential for aligning mathematics with scientific practice.
